name: Caviar extract

card.summary: A luxury skincare and supplement ingredient made from sturgeon roe, studied for hydration, wrinkles and pigmentation to give smoother, brighter-looking skin.
card.note: Most studies are lab or animal work; human data is limited to a few trials.

quick.overview:
Caviar extract is made from sturgeon eggs and used in premium skin creams and, in some forms, as an oral supplement. It is marketed for firmer, smoother, more even skin, drawing on phospholipids such as DHA and low-molecular-weight peptides.

Lab and mouse studies report reduced UV-related skin aging, less melanin production and effects on collagen-related pathways. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of an enzyme-treated supercritical caviar extract measured skin elasticity, wrinkles and hydration at 4 and 8 weeks.
quick.how: It appears as an ingredient in creams and serums, and as an oral extract in the studied trial. Use is typically as part of a daily skincare routine alongside other products.
quick.risks: Safety information is limited to trial reporting and general ingredient use. People allergic to fish or fish roe may react to products that contain it, and it is an animal-derived ingredient.

lead: Caviar extract is derived from caviar, the salt-cured roe of sturgeon, and is used as a cosmetic and nutritional ingredient. Caviar itself is traditionally the roe of Caspian and Black Sea sturgeon, and overfishing led to export limits and CITES restrictions in the 2000s, which spurred farmed production.[1]

For looks, caviar extract is promoted for skin that looks firmer, more hydrated and more even in tone. A 2020 laboratory study reported that caviar extract and its component DHA promoted adipocyte differentiation and adiponectin production and was associated with reduced matrix metalloproteinase-1 expression in UVB-irradiated skin models.[2]
In humans, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of an enzyme-treated supercritical caviar extract, taken orally, measured elasticity, wrinkles and hydration at 4 and 8 weeks.[3]

chain: Extract supplies DHA phospholipids and peptides
Lab studies report less UV-driven collagen breakdown and melanin production
Claimed result: firmer, more even, hydrated skin
angle.text: Used topically or orally for an anti-aging, brightening effect. Most mechanism data come from cell and mouse studies, with a few human trial measurements of skin elasticity and wrinkles.

infobox: Randomized placebo-controlled trial of enzyme-treated extract (2023)

paras: Caviar is about half water with protein and fat, and is a source of vitamin B12 as food.[1] The extracts studied for skin are processed forms: one enzyme-treated supercritical extract is mainly composed of low-molecular-weight peptides rich in leucine, tyrosine and phenylalanine.[3]

In UVB-irradiated hairless mice and melanoma cells, enzyme-treated caviar extract lowered melanin content and reduced levels of melanogenesis signalling proteins such as MITF and tyrosinase.[4] A 2025 study with an acid-protease-treated extract reported antioxidant activity in cells and reduced photoaging damage in mice, with effects on NF-kB and MMP pathways and on collagen-related markers.[5] These findings are preclinical.
Caviar is described in research papers as having moved from a nutritional food into cosmetic products.[2] It is positioned as a luxury ingredient in creams and serums.

A 2023 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Nutrients assessed an enzyme-treated supercritical caviar extract by measuring skin elasticity, wrinkles and hydration at 4 and 8 weeks of oral use.[3] Wider human evidence on caviar-based skincare products is limited.
